Q11_11_TEXT: I tend to work on novel groups, so find data equivalency that is germane to the study and then locating it (I have no institutional affiliations beyond a loose one with a distant museum) can be a trial at times. The fact I have well connected colleagues does allow this to be overcome, and open access makes a huge difference, however it can add time to the process of accumulating, reviewing and internalizing trait data that is relevant to a specific piece of research. The fact this is often occurring in a  remote location adds a little to this dynamic. On the other hand, the flexibility this allows me, due to a lack of institutional rules and oversight more than makes up for this time-input, as it allows me (as an quasi-independent researcher) to avoid a whole layer of time consuming, inflexible rules and protocols in terms of my travels, reporting and activities.

Q15_6_TEXT: This is an interesting question. As I mentioned in a previous question, most of my efforts are made as a collaborator in green-fields or project driven (via a consultancy) team-based efforts. This often involves me doing significant field studies in remote areas as I do discovery collections, observe basic biology and then explore complex interactive ecology, as well as make molecular preparations and undertake other activities as I or others suggest them. This often involves me proactively designing protocols in the field, with input (often via email) coming from colleagues as they refine and research methods to obtain useful data that has methodological stability and usefulness which will inform the end-point research. by it's nature, this can mean re-visiting apparent significant findings, especially in terms of apparent interesting ecological data, or else presenting these observations with caveats which possibly do not reflect the level of research certainty that the group (or members of the group) have in them. While standardized methodology as regards trait data collection is and potentially would be a valuable tool in undertaking this work, I think there will always be situations where, due to time constraints, broad project parameters and task prioritisation along the unusual nature of some previously unknown and undescribed interactive ecology, where innovation in the space of trait collection, or acceptance of a less than perfect study outcome based on available resources will be a reality in at least some of the work I have been a participant in.
